claims.claim: Cyclin B1 was proposed to be actively transcribed during mitosis.
claims.source: In line with this hypothesis, the master mitotic regulator Cyclin B1 was proposed to be actively transcribed during mitosis and to be required to sustain a robust SAC response (Mena et al., 2010; Sciortino et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Centromere assembly has been proposed to depend on transcription of centromeric α-satellite DNA.
claims.source: Centromere assembly, which underlies the catalytic mechanism behind the SAC, has also been recently proposed to depend on transcription of centromeric α-satellite DNA and to be regulated by non-coding RNAs (Blower, 2016; Carone et al., 2009; Chan et al., 2012; Du et al., 2010; Grenfell et al., 2016; Li et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2015; Nakano et al., 2003; Pezer and Ugarković, 2008; Rošić et al., 2014; Topp et al., 2004; Wong et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The centromeric localization and activation of Aurora B was shown to be dependent on centromeric transcription.
claims.source: In particular, the centromeric localization and activation of Aurora B, the catalytic subunit of the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC) required for SAC response and error correction during mitosis (Carmena et al., 2012; Santaguida et al., 2011) was shown to be dependent on centromeric transcription (Blower, 2016; Grenfell et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Over 8000 transcripts are expressed de novo during mitosis and mitotic exit.
claims.source: Finally, a recent study using pulse-labeling of nascent transcripts and RNA-seq of mitotic-enriched cell populations reported that over 8000 transcripts are expressed de novo during mitosis and mitotic exit to prepare cells for the subsequent interphase (Palozola et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Cells treated with nocodazole remained in mitosis for 19.2 ± 7.0 hr.
claims.source: Consistent with previous observations in fixed cells (Becker et al., 2010), we found that live cells treated with nocodazole remained in mitosis for 19.2 ± 7.0 hr (median ± SD, n = 386 cells), whereas cells treated with nocodazole followed by actinomycin D persisted in mitosis for only 16.1 ± 5.6 hr (n = 301 cells, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1B,C and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Cells treated with nocodazole followed by actinomycin D persisted in mitosis for only 16.1 ± 5.6 hr.
claims.source: Consistent with previous observations in fixed cells (Becker et al., 2010), we found that live cells treated with nocodazole remained in mitosis for 19.2 ± 7.0 hr (median ± SD, n = 386 cells), whereas cells treated with nocodazole followed by actinomycin D persisted in mitosis for only 16.1 ± 5.6 hr (n = 301 cells, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1B,C and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Approximately 90% of nocodazole-treated cells died after a prolonged mitotic delay.
claims.source: Interestingly, approximately 90% of nocodazole-treated cells died after a prolonged mitotic delay, whereas 54% of the cells treated with nocodazole and actinomycin D underwent mitotic slippage (Rieder and Maiato, 2004) (Figure 1B,D and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: 54% of the cells treated with nocodazole and actinomycin D underwent mitotic slippage.
claims.source: Interestingly, approximately 90% of nocodazole-treated cells died after a prolonged mitotic delay, whereas 54% of the cells treated with nocodazole and actinomycin D underwent mitotic slippage (Rieder and Maiato, 2004) (Figure 1B,D and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Treatment with actinomycin D compromises the capacity of cells to sustain a prolonged mitotic delay.
claims.source: Thus, treatment with actinomycin D compromises the capacity of cells to sustain a prolonged mitotic delay and interferes with their fate.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the live-cell imaging data showing reduced mitotic duration and altered cell fate.

claims.claim: Slower Cyclin B1 degradation promotes mitotic cell death.
claims.source: The relationship between the capacity to sustain a robust SAC response and the subsequent cell fate after a mitotic delay has been shown to depend on the kinetics of anaphase-promoting complex (APC)-mediated Cyclin B1 degradation, with slower degradation promoting mitotic cell death, and faster degradation promoting mitotic slippage (Brito and Rieder, 2006; Gascoigne and Taylor, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Faster Cyclin B1 degradation promotes mitotic slippage.
claims.source: The relationship between the capacity to sustain a robust SAC response and the subsequent cell fate after a mitotic delay has been shown to depend on the kinetics of anaphase-promoting complex (APC)-mediated Cyclin B1 degradation, with slower degradation promoting mitotic cell death, and faster degradation promoting mitotic slippage (Brito and Rieder, 2006; Gascoigne and Taylor, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Cells treated with nocodazole and MG132 increased the mitotic delay relative to cells treated only with nocodazole from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 30.1 ± 14.7 hr.
claims.source: Accordingly, cells treated with nocodazole and MG132 increased the mitotic delay relative to cells treated only with nocodazole (from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 30.1 ± 14.7 hr, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C and Video 1), and caused cell death in mitosis in 100% of the cases (Figure 1D and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Nocodazole and MG132 treatment caused cell death in mitosis in 100% of the cases.
claims.source: Accordingly, cells treated with nocodazole and MG132 increased the mitotic delay relative to cells treated only with nocodazole (from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 30.1 ± 14.7 hr, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C and Video 1), and caused cell death in mitosis in 100% of the cases (Figure 1D and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Acute SAC inactivation through Mps1 inhibition after nocodazole treatment significantly decreased the mitotic delay from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 5.4 ± 2.6 hr.
claims.source: Conversely, acute SAC inactivation through Mps1 inhibition after nocodazole treatment significantly decreased the mitotic delay relative to nocodazole-treated cells (from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 5.4 ± 2.6 hr, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C and Video 1), and caused almost immediate mitotic slippage in 100% of the cells (Figure 1D and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Mps1 inhibition after nocodazole treatment caused almost immediate mitotic slippage in 100% of the cells.
claims.source: Conversely, acute SAC inactivation through Mps1 inhibition after nocodazole treatment significantly decreased the mitotic delay relative to nocodazole-treated cells (from 19.2 ± 7.0 hr to 5.4 ± 2.6 hr, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C and Video 1), and caused almost immediate mitotic slippage in 100% of the cells (Figure 1D and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Proteasome inhibition with MG132 reverted the Mps1 inhibition phenotype, increasing mitotic duration and switching cell fate from mitotic slippage to death.
claims.source: Proteasome inhibition with MG132 reverted the Mps1 inhibition phenotype, increasing mitotic duration and switching cell fate from mitotic slippage to death (p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C,D and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The ability of actinomycin D to reduce the mitotic delay and induce slippage in cells treated with nocodazole was rescued after inhibition of proteasome activity with MG132.
claims.source: Most important, the ability of actinomycin D to reduce the mitotic delay and induce slippage in cells treated with nocodazole was rescued after inhibition of proteasome activity with MG132 (p≤0.01, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 1C,D and Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D compromises SAC response in a proteasome-dependent manner.
claims.source: Overall, these experiments suggest that actinomycin D compromises SAC response and the capacity to sustain a prolonged mitotic delay, in a proteasome-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue experiments with MG132.

claims.claim: Cyclin B1-Venus fluorescence decayed very slowly in the presence of nocodazole, likely due to residual APC activity.
claims.source: In agreement with previous reports, Cyclin B1-Venus fluorescence decayed very slowly in the presence of nocodazole, likely due to residual APC activity (Figure 1F) (Brito and Rieder, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1F and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Treatment of nocodazole-arrested cells with actinomycin D caused a faster decline in Cyclin B1-Venus.
claims.source: Treatment of nocodazole-arrested cells with actinomycin D caused a faster decline in Cyclin B1-Venus (p<0.0001, Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA), Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Cyclin B1-Venus levels in nocodazole-treated cells remained constant for several hours after inhibition of the proteasome with MG132, regardless of the presence of actinomycin D.
claims.source: Interestingly, Cyclin B1-Venus levels in nocodazole-treated cells remained constant for several hours after inhibition of the proteasome with MG132, regardless of the presence of actinomycin D (p≤0.05, ANCOVA, Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D compromises SAC robustness and the capacity to prevent APC-mediated Cyclin B1 degradation, independently of de novo transcription.
claims.source: We concluded that actinomycin D compromises SAC robustness and the capacity to prevent APC-mediated Cyclin B1 degradation, independently of de novo transcription.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the Cyclin B1 degradation experiments and the lack of effect on transcript levels.

claims.claim: Addition of actinomycin D for 8 hr in cells pre-treated with nocodazole reduced or abolished pH3S10 accumulation in approximately 17% of the nocodazole-treated cells.
claims.source: In contrast with nocodazole-treatment in which all mitotic cells showed high levels of pH3S10, addition of actinomycin D reduced or abolished pH3S10 accumulation in approximately 17% of the nocodazole-treated cells (Figure 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Cells with reduced/abolished pH3S10 after actinomycin D treatment still showed signs of chromosome condensation indistinguishable from neighbouring cells with normal levels of pH3S10.
claims.source: Importantly, these cells still showed signs of chromosome condensation (as determined by DAPI staining of DNA) that were indistinguishable from neighbouring cells with normal levels of pH3S10 (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The observed reduction/abolishment of pH3S10 was not associated with a pre-apoptotic state.
claims.source: Moreover, the observed reduction/abolishment of pH3S10 was not associated with a pre-apoptotic state, as those cells were negative for a cleaved form of caspase 3 (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2A showing absence of cleaved caspase 3.

claims.claim: Cells with reduced/abolished pH3S10 after actinomycin D treatment showed abnormally low levels of total Aurora B and its active phosphorylated form on Threonine 232.
claims.source: In line with the observed reduction/abolishment of pH3S10, these cells also showed abnormally low levels of total Aurora B and its active phosphorylated form on Threonine 232 (Yasui et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2A and citation to previous work on Aurora B phosphorylation.

claims.claim: In nocodazole- and actinomycin D-treated cells that showed high levels of pH3S10, Aurora B, including its active form, was found displaced along the chromosome arms.
claims.source: Noteworthy, even in those nocodazole- and actinomycin D-treated cells that showed high levels of pH3S10, Aurora B, including its active form, was found displaced along the chromosome arms (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D compromises normal Aurora B localization and activity.
claims.source: Thus, actinomycin D compromises normal Aurora B localization and activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing Aurora B mislocalization and reduced activity.

claims.claim: Addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 45% reduction of Mad1 at the outer kinetochore.
claims.source: We found that addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 45% reduction of Mad1 at the outer kinetochore (Figure 2C,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2C,E.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr did not affect the kinetochore localization of active Mps1 (Mps1 pT676).
claims.source: Importantly, actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr did not affect the kinetochore localization of active Mps1 (Mps1 pT676; (Jelluma et al., 2008)) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B) or the phosphorylation of histone H3 at threonine 3 (H3T3p), a proxy for Haspin activity previously implicated in Aurora B recruitment to centromeres (Kelly et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr did not affect the phosphorylation of histone H3 at threonine 3 (H3T3p).
claims.source: Importantly, actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr did not affect the kinetochore localization of active Mps1 (Mps1 pT676; (Jelluma et al., 2008)) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B) or the phosphorylation of histone H3 at threonine 3 (H3T3p), a proxy for Haspin activity previously implicated in Aurora B recruitment to centromeres (Kelly et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D compromises the normal localization of Aurora B at centromeres and SAC proteins to unattached kinetochores, independently of an effect over Mps1 and Haspin kinase activity.
claims.source: Taken together, these experiments show that actinomycin D compromises the normal localization of Aurora B at centromeres and SAC proteins to unattached kinetochores, independently of an effect over Mps1 and Haspin kinase activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing no effect on Mps1 and Haspin activity.

claims.claim: Addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 22% reduction in phosphorylation levels of Knl1.
claims.source: Consistent with an attenuation of Aurora B activity at centromeres, we found that addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 22% and 43% reduction on the phosphorylation levels of Knl1 and Dsn1 (a member of the Mis12 complex), respectively (Figure 3A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 43% reduction in phosphorylation levels of Dsn1.
claims.source: Consistent with an attenuation of Aurora B activity at centromeres, we found that addition of actinomycin D for 4 hr to nocodazole-treated cells led to a 22% and 43% reduction on the phosphorylation levels of Knl1 and Dsn1 (a member of the Mis12 complex), respectively (Figure 3A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D treatment led to a 29% reduction in total Knl1.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also found a 29% reduction in total Knl1 (Figure 3E,F), whereas total Dsn1, Hec1 (a member of the Ndc80 complex) and CENP-A were unaffected by actinomycin D treatment (Figure 3G,H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Total Dsn1, Hec1 and CENP-A were unaffected by actinomycin D treatment.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also found a 29% reduction in total Knl1 (Figure 3E,F), whereas total Dsn1, Hec1 (a member of the Ndc80 complex) and CENP-A were unaffected by actinomycin D treatment (Figure 3G,H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Perturbation of Aurora B centromeric localization by actinomycin D translates into a local reduction of activity and the consequent decrease in phosphorylation of key Aurora B substrates at the kinetochore.
claims.source: Thus, perturbation of Aurora B centromeric localization by actinomycin D translates into a local reduction of activity and the consequent decrease in phosphorylation of key Aurora B substrates at the kinetochore.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing reduced phosphorylation of Aurora B substrates.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr compromises the recruitment of Knl1 to unattached kinetochores.
claims.source: Moreover, while actinomycin D treatment for 4 hr does not perturb the normal localization of CENP-A and members of the Ndc80 and Mis12 complex, it compromises the recruitment of Knl1 to unattached kinetochores.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing reduced Knl1 levels at kinetochores.

claims.claim: Aurora B inhibition in nocodazole-treated cells caused a 38% reduction of Mad1 at unattached kinetochores.
claims.source: We found that, similar to actinomycin D treatment, Aurora B inhibition in nocodazole-treated cells caused a 38% and 28% reduction of Mad1 and Knl1 at unattached kinetochores, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Aurora B inhibition in nocodazole-treated cells caused a 28% reduction of Knl1 at unattached kinetochores.
claims.source: We found that, similar to actinomycin D treatment, Aurora B inhibition in nocodazole-treated cells caused a 38% and 28% reduction of Mad1 and Knl1 at unattached kinetochores, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Constitutive targeting of Aurora B to centromeres by expressing a Cenp-B-INCENP fusion protein was able to rescue SAC response in actinomycin D-treated cells.
claims.source: Importantly, it has previously been shown that constitutive targeting of Aurora B to centromeres by expressing a Cenp-B-INCENP fusion protein was able to rescue SAC response in actinomycin D-treated cells (Becker et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Perturbation of Aurora B localization and consequent decrease in activity at centromeres is the primary effect of Actinomycin D treatment.
claims.source: Overall, these data suggest that perturbation of Aurora B localization and consequent decrease in activity at centromeres is the primary effect of Actinomycin D treatment and this likely accounts for the weakened SAC response due to a downstream effect over Knl1 and Mad1 recruitment.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results showing Aurora B mislocalization and downstream effects on Knl1 and Mad1.

claims.claim: Aurora B, Survivin and Borealin total protein levels remained unchanged after 4 hr treatment with actinomycin D.
claims.source: Western blot analysis revealed that Aurora B, as well as the total protein levels of the CPC regulatory subunits Survivin and Borealin remained unchanged relative to controls (including inhibition of translation during mitosis with cycloheximide or Aurora B inhibition with ZM447439) after 4 hr treatment with actinomycin D (Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Quantitative transcriptome analysis did not reveal any significant changes in annotated or novel assembled transcripts upon actinomycin D treatment.
claims.source: Our quantitative transcriptome analysis did not reveal any significant changes either in annotated or novel assembled transcripts (including all biotypes) upon actinomycin D treatment, ruling out differential gene expression after transcription inhibition during mitosis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Cyclin B1 and all key mitotic regulators, including Aurora B, were not de novo transcribed even during a prolonged mitosis.
claims.source: Importantly, we confirmed that Cyclin B1, as well as all key mitotic regulators, including Aurora B, were not de novo transcribed even during a prolonged mitosis (Figure 4D; see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D treatment did not reduce the level of centromeric α-satellite RNA.
claims.source: We found that actinomycin D treatment did not reduce the level of centromeric α-satellite RNA (Figure 4E,F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 4E,F.

claims.claim: Inhibition of transcription with actinomycin D during a prolonged mitosis does not impair normal transcript levels, including centromeric α-satellite RNA, nor the normal levels of CPC proteins.
claims.source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that inhibition of transcription with actinomycin D during a prolonged mitosis caused by persistently unattached kinetochores does not impair normal transcript levels, including centromeric α-satellite RNA, nor the normal levels of CPC proteins.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined RNA-seq, qPCR, and Western blot data.

claims.claim: α-amanitin did not cause any significant effect over Mcl1 transcript levels relative to controls.
claims.source: As suspected, we could not detect any significant effect of α-amanitin over Mcl1 transcript levels relative to controls (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Treatment with either actinomycin D or triptolide resulted in a 5-fold decrease in Mcl1 transcript levels.
claims.source: In sharp contrast, treatment with either actinomycin D or triptolide resulted in a 5-fold decrease in Mcl1 transcript levels (Figure 5A) and led interphase cells to death within 4–5 hr in the presence of either actinomycin D or triptolide (Videos 1 and 2), suggesting an efficient and equivalent inhibition of transcription in both scenarios.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Triptolide, but not α-amanitin, caused the degradation of the large subunit of RNA Polymerase II.
claims.source: Finally, we confirmed that, within the time course of our experiment, triptolide, but not α-amanitin, caused the degradation of the large subunit of RNA Polymerase II (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Triptolide efficiently inhibits transcription in living cells independently of DNA intercalation.
claims.source: Thus, triptolide, but not α-amanitin, efficiently inhibits transcription in living cells and it does so independently of DNA intercalation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the qPCR and Western blot data showing efficient transcription inhibition by triptolide without DNA intercalation.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in mitotic duration between nocodazole-treated cells with or without triptolide (19.3 ± 7.1 hr vs 19.5 ± 5.8 hr).
claims.source: We found no significant differences in mitotic duration between nocodazole-treated cells with or without triptolide (19.3 ± 7.1 hr vs 19.5 ± 5.8 hr, respectively, median ±SD, n = 301 cells, p=0.65, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 5B and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Triptolide did not cause the displacement of Aurora B from centromeres in both fixed and live-cell assays.
claims.source: Triptolide also did not cause the displacement of Aurora B from centromeres in both fixed and live-cell assays (Figure 5D–G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 5D–G.

claims.claim: SAC robustness, Aurora B centromeric localization, and the capacity to die in mitosis after a prolonged mitotic delay is independent of de novo transcription.
claims.source: These results, supported by our RNA-seq data, indicate that SAC robustness, Aurora B centromeric localization, as well as the capacity to die in mitosis after a prolonged mitotic delay is independent of de novo transcription.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the triptolide experiments showing no effect on Aurora B localization or SAC response.

claims.claim: Mcl1 transcript levels were only slightly decreased (without statistic significance) after 4 hr of ethidium bromide treatment.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that interphase cells were able to enter mitosis after treatment with ethidium bromide (Video 2). Additionally, Mcl1 transcript levels were only slightly decreased (without statistic significance) after 4 hr of ethidium bromide treatment (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Cells treated with nocodazole and ethidium bromide spent slightly less time in mitosis when compared to cells treated with nocodazole only (19.2 ± 7.0 hr vs 18.1 ± 5.9 hr), but the difference was not statistically relevant.
claims.source: In agreement, cells treated with nocodazole and ethidium bromide spent slightly less time in mitosis when compared to cells treated with nocodazole only, but the difference was not statistically relevant (19.2 ± 7.0 hr vs 18.1 ± 5.9 hr, median ±SD, n = 386;151 cells/condition, p=0.13, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 6B and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Ethidium bromide caused a significant effect over cell fate after the mitotic delay imposed by nocodazole, causing mitotic slippage in approximately 50% of the cells.
claims.source: However, similar to actinomycin D, ethidium bromide caused a significant effect over cell fate after the mitotic delay imposed by nocodazole, causing mitotic slippage in approximately 50% of the cells (Figure 6C and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Ethidium bromide displaced Aurora B from centromeres in fixed cells, although to a less extent when compared with actinomycin D.
claims.source: Ethidium bromide also displaced Aurora B from centromeres in fixed cells, although to a less extent when compared with actinomycin D (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 6D,E.

claims.claim: DNA intercalating drugs interfere with normal Aurora B localization at centromeres and compromise cell fate after a prolonged mitosis.
claims.source: These data suggest that DNA intercalating drugs interfere with normal Aurora B localization at centromeres and compromise cell fate after a prolonged mitosis.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the ethidium bromide experiments showing Aurora B mislocalization and altered cell fate.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D or ethidium bromide-treated NCPs showed ~50% reduction in CPC-CTM binding, when compared to DMSO- or Triptolide-treated NCPs.
claims.source: Consistent with our fixed and live-cell data, actinomycin D or ethidium bromide-treated NCPs showed ~50% reduction in CPC-CTM binding, when compared to DMSO- or Triptolide-treated NCPs (p≤0.05, t test, Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data presented in Figure 6F,G.

claims.claim: DNA intercalating drugs interfere with centromere integrity.
claims.source: Thus, DNA intercalating drugs interfere with centromere integrity.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the EMSA data showing reduced CPC binding to nucleosomes.

claims.claim: Control and triptolide-treated cells took a similar time to exit mitosis after nocodazole washout (79.1 ± 28.7 min vs 86.2 ± 31.7 min).
claims.source: We found that control and triptolide-treated cells took a similar time to exit mitosis after nocodazole washout (79.1 ± 28.7 min vs 86.2 ± 31.7 min, median ± SD, n = 116;113 cells/condition, p=0.11, Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test, Figure 7C and Video 3) without any apparent defect (Figure 7D and Video 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D-treated cells showed a significant delay in mitotic exit after nocodazole washout.
claims.source: In contrast, actinomycin D-treated cells showed a significant delay in mitotic exit (Figure 7C and Video 3) and underwent mitotic slippage (33%) or failed cytokinesis (47%) (Figure 7D and Video 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D-treated cells underwent mitotic slippage (33%) or failed cytokinesis (47%) after nocodazole washout.
claims.source: In contrast, actinomycin D-treated cells showed a significant delay in mitotic exit (Figure 7C and Video 3) and underwent mitotic slippage (33%) or failed cytokinesis (47%) (Figure 7D and Video 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D-treated cells after nocodazole washout showed persistent DNA bridges at the cleavage furrow.
claims.source: Close inspection of actinomycin D-treated cells after nocodazole washout by immunofluorescence revealed persistent DNA bridges at the cleavage furrow (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which might have accounted for the observed failure in completing cytokinesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The capacity of human cells to progress and exit mitosis, including the completion of cytokinesis, is independent of de novo transcription.
claims.source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that the capacity of human cells to progress and exit mitosis, including the completion of cytokinesis, is independent of de novo transcription.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the nocodazole washout experiments showing normal mitotic progression with triptolide.

claims.claim: The capacity of human cells to sustain, progress, exit or die in mitosis does not require de novo transcription.
claims.source: By combining direct live-cell imaging, while monitoring the efficiency and specificity of transcription inhibition at the whole genome level, we show that the capacity of human cells to sustain, progress, exit or die in mitosis does not require de novo transcription.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results with triptolide showing no effect on mitotic outcomes.

claims.claim: Actinomycin D and other DNA intercalating agents caused partial dissociation of the CPC from nucleosomes.
claims.source: Actinomycin D and other DNA intercalating agents caused partial dissociation of the CPC from nucleosomes, thereby compromising Aurora B centromeric localization and SAC response.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data showing reduced CPC binding to nucleosomes.

claims.claim: α-amanitin failed to efficiently inhibit transcription even after several hours in mitosis.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing no effect on Mcl1 transcript levels.

claims.claim: Efficient inhibition of mitotic transcription independently of DNA intercalation using triptolide had no discernible effect over Aurora B centromeric localization or SAC response.
claims.source: Most importantly, efficient inhibition of mitotic transcription independently of DNA intercalation using triptolide had no discernible effect over Aurora B centromeric localization or SAC response.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and live-cell imaging data with triptolide.

claims.claim: Centromere integrity, rather than mitotic transcription, is required for proper localization and activity of Aurora B and to mount a robust SAC.
claims.source: We concluded that centromere integrity, rather than mitotic transcription, is required for proper localization and activity of Aurora B and to mount a robust SAC able to sustain mitosis in human cells for several hours in the event of unattached kinetochores.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results showing that DNA intercalation, not transcription inhibition, affects Aurora B and SAC.

claims.claim: Aurora B activity and its stable association with centromeres are important for normal Knl1 and Mad1 recruitment to unattached kinetochores.
claims.source: Accordingly, we showed that both Aurora B activity and its stable association with centromeres are important for normal Knl1 and Mad1 recruitment to unattached kinetochores.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing reduced Knl1 and Mad1 levels after Aurora B perturbation.

claims.claim: RNA Polymerase II is generally found displaced from chromatin during prometaphase.
claims.source: Consistent with a global shut-down of transcription during prometaphase (the physiological equivalent of nocodazole-arrested cells), RNA Polymerase II is generally found displaced from chromatin (Hsiung et al., 2016), with the notorious exception of the centromeric region (Chan et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Centromeric transcription is involved in nucleosome disassembly during interphase.
claims.source: Centromeric transcription is involved in nucleosome disassembly during interphase (Boeger et al., 2003) to facilitate the replacement of histone H3 by CENP-A (McKittrick et al., 2004; Tagami et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Regardless of the capacity to detect residual transcription during mitosis, this is not required for human cells to sustain, progress, exit or die in mitosis.
claims.source: Overall, our results demonstrate that, regardless of our capacity to detect residual transcription that might still take place on specific chromosomal loci during mitosis, this is not required for human cells to sustain, progress, exit or die in mitosis.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results showing normal mitotic outcomes with triptolide treatment.

results.result: Actinomycin D treatment reduces mitotic duration in nocodazole-arrested cells from 19.2±7.0 hr to 16.1±5.6 hr and alters cell fate, with 54% undergoing mitotic slippage versus 90% death in controls. This effect is rescued by proteasome inhibition with MG132, suggesting actinomycin D compromises SAC response in a proteasome-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C31 provide converging evidence from live-cell imaging with appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney, p<0.0001) and adequate sample sizes (n=301-386 cells). The rescue experiments with MG132 and Mps1 inhibitor provide strong mechanistic support. The data consistently show actinomycin D effects on mitotic timing and cell fate that are reversed by proteasome inhibition.

results.result: Actinomycin D accelerates Cyclin B1 degradation in nocodazole-arrested cells, but this effect is blocked by proteasome inhibition with MG132. The authors conclude this occurs independently of de novo transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 show clear effects on Cyclin B1 degradation kinetics with appropriate statistical analysis (ANCOVA, p<0.0001). However, C35's conclusion that this is 'independent of de novo transcription' is premature at this stage, as the transcription-independence is only established later with triptolide experiments. The mechanistic link between actinomycin D treatment and transcription-independence requires additional evidence.

results.result: Actinomycin D treatment causes Aurora B mislocalization from centromeres and reduces Mad1 recruitment to kinetochores (45% reduction) without affecting Mps1 or Haspin activity. In ~17% of cells, pH3S10 is reduced/abolished while chromosome condensation remains normal.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C45 are well-supported by immunofluorescence data with appropriate quantification and statistical analysis. The observation that Mps1 and Haspin activity are unaffected (C43-C44) strengthens the specificity of the Aurora B effect. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=258-474 kinetochores) and controls are appropriate. The phenotypic characterization is thorough.

results.result: Actinomycin D reduces phosphorylation of Aurora B substrates Knl1 (22%) and Dsn1 (43%), and decreases total Knl1 levels (29%) without affecting Dsn1, Hec1, or CENP-A. Aurora B inhibition produces similar effects on Mad1 (38% reduction) and Knl1 (28% reduction), suggesting Aurora B mislocalization is the primary mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C55 provide strong mechanistic evidence linking Aurora B mislocalization to downstream effects on kinetochore proteins. The parallel experiments with Aurora B inhibitor (C52-C53) strengthen the causal interpretation. The selectivity (some proteins affected, others not) supports specificity. Citation to rescue experiments (C54) from prior work adds support. Statistical analysis appears appropriate.

results.result: Actinomycin D treatment does not alter total protein levels of Aurora B, Survivin, or Borealin, nor does it change transcript levels of mitotic regulators including Cyclin B1, Aurora B, or centromeric α-satellite RNA, as measured by Western blot, RNA-seq, and qPCR.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 provide multiple lines of evidence (Western blot, RNA-seq, qPCR) showing no changes in protein or transcript levels. The RNA-seq analysis appears comprehensive, examining both annotated and novel transcripts. The qPCR validation for α-satellite RNA addresses a specific hypothesis about centromeric transcription. However, RNA-seq has limitations for repetitive centromeric regions, which the authors acknowledge.

results.result: Triptolide, a non-DNA-intercalating transcription inhibitor, efficiently reduces Mcl1 transcripts (5-fold) and causes RNA Pol II degradation, but does not affect mitotic duration (19.3±7.1 vs 19.5±5.8 hr), Aurora B localization, or cell fate in nocodazole-arrested cells. In contrast, α-amanitin fails to inhibit transcription effectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C67 provide the critical control experiment distinguishing transcription inhibition from DNA intercalation effects. The comparison of three inhibitors (actinomycin D, triptolide, α-amanitin) with different mechanisms is well-designed. Triptolide's efficacy is validated by Mcl1 reduction and Pol II degradation (C62-C63), while its lack of effect on mitotic parameters (C65-C66) is clearly demonstrated. This is the key experiment supporting the main conclusion.

results.result: Ethidium bromide, a DNA intercalator that does not inhibit transcription (Mcl1 levels unchanged), causes Aurora B displacement from centromeres and induces mitotic slippage in ~50% of cells, similar to actinomycin D. EMSA experiments show ~50% reduction in CPC binding to nucleosomes with actinomycin D or ethidium bromide but not triptolide.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 provide strong mechanistic evidence that DNA intercalation, not transcription inhibition, causes Aurora B mislocalization. The EMSA experiments (C73) directly demonstrate reduced CPC-nucleosome binding with DNA intercalators but not triptolide, providing molecular-level support. The ethidium bromide control is well-chosen as it intercalates DNA without inhibiting transcription. Statistical analysis is appropriate (t-test, p≤0.05).

results.result: After nocodazole washout, triptolide-treated cells exit mitosis normally (86.2±31.7 min vs 79.1±28.7 min control), while actinomycin D-treated cells show delayed exit and defects including mitotic slippage (33%) and cytokinesis failure (47%) with persistent DNA bridges.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 demonstrate that transcription inhibition without DNA intercalation does not impair mitotic progression or exit. The nocodazole washout experiment is well-designed to test mitotic progression capacity. Statistical analysis is appropriate (Mann-Whitney, p=0.11 for triptolide vs control). The observation of DNA bridges in actinomycin D-treated cells (C78) provides a plausible mechanism for cytokinesis failure.

results.result: The main conclusion is that mitotic progression, arrest, exit, and death are determined by centromere structural integrity rather than de novo transcription. DNA intercalating drugs (actinomycin D, ethidium bromide) compromise Aurora B localization and SAC signaling by reducing CPC-nucleosome interactions, while transcription inhibition without DNA intercalation (triptolide) has no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C10, C80-C84, and C91 represent the paper's central conclusion, which is well-supported by the convergence of multiple experimental approaches: (1) differential effects of actinomycin D vs triptolide, (2) ethidium bromide phenocopying actinomycin D, (3) EMSA showing direct effects on CPC-nucleosome binding, (4) lack of transcriptional changes by RNA-seq/qPCR, and (5) normal mitotic progression with triptolide. The logic is sound and the evidence is compelling.

results.result: Prior work has proposed that transcription is required for SAC response, with specific claims about Cyclin B1 transcription during mitosis, centromeric transcription regulating Aurora B, and over 8000 transcripts expressed de novo during mitosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C11-C17 accurately represent prior literature through appropriate citations. These claims establish the context and rationale for the current study by summarizing the prevailing hypotheses that the authors are testing. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization of prior work is fair.

results.result: Prior work has shown that slower Cyclin B1 degradation promotes mitotic cell death while faster degradation promotes mitotic slippage.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 accurately cite prior work establishing the relationship between Cyclin B1 degradation kinetics and cell fate. This provides important context for interpreting the actinomycin D effects on Cyclin B1 degradation and cell fate observed in the current study.

results.result: α-amanitin failed to efficiently inhibit transcription even after several hours in mitosis, as evidenced by lack of effect on Mcl1 transcript levels.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is supported by qPCR data (C61) showing no significant effect on Mcl1 levels. This negative result is important for interpreting prior studies using α-amanitin and explains why the authors chose triptolide as the non-intercalating transcription inhibitor. The explanation about α-amanitin being a slow-uptake drug provides mechanistic context.

results.result: Aurora B activity and stable centromeric association are important for normal Knl1 and Mad1 recruitment to unattached kinetochores.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 is supported by the parallel effects of actinomycin D and Aurora B inhibitor on Knl1 and Mad1 levels (C42, C46-C48, C52-C53). This represents a mechanistic insight into how Aurora B mislocalization affects SAC signaling, though the specific molecular mechanisms are not fully elucidated.

results.result: Prior work has shown that RNA Polymerase II localizes to centromeres during prometaphase, centromeric transcription is involved in nucleosome disassembly during interphase, and α-satellite RNA levels must be tightly regulated for faithful mitosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 accurately represent prior literature on centromeric transcription and its proposed roles. These claims provide important context for the discussion of why centromeric transcription might occur and how it could affect centromere function, even though the current study shows it is not required during mitosis.
